title: Muhammad al-Bukhari
wiki_lead:
Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm al-Juʿfī al-Bukhārī (Arabic: أبو عبد الله محمد بن إسماعيل بن إبرهيم الجعفي البخاري; 21 July 810 C.E – 1 September 870; AH 194–256), commonly known as al-Bukhārī, was a Persian Tajik 9th-century Muslim muhaddith and one of the foremost authorities on hadith, widely regarded as the most important hadith scholar in the history of Sunni Islam. 
Born in Bukhara, in present-day Uzbekistan, he began studying hadith at the age of ten and became noted for his exceptional memory. He travelled extensively throughout the Abbasid Caliphate in search of traditions and studied under numerous influential contemporary scholars. He is said to have interviewed about a thousand shaykhs and examined more than 200,000 hadiths, rejecting many after careful scrutiny at a time when numerous spurious traditions were in circulation.
Al-Bukhārī memorized thousands of hadith narrations and compiled his principal collection, the Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, in 846 C.E. The work selected 7563 narrations including repetitions, from over 600,000 narrations, but fewer than 3,000 when repeated material is excluded; its contents are arranged principally by subject for ease of reference in ninety-seven "books", subdivided into 3,450 chapters. He spent the remainder of his life teaching the traditions he had collected. Near the end of his life he was exiled from Nishapur and subsequently moved to Khartank, near Samarkand.
The Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī became the most highly revered hadith collection in Sunni Islam. Together with the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī's student Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 875; AH 261), it is known collectively as the Ṣaḥīḥayn (Arabic: صحيحين, romanized: Saḥiḥayn). The two collections are regarded by Sunnis as the principal definitive compilations of reliable hadith and, after the Qurʾān, as authoritative sources for principles of legislation and religious practice. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī is also one of the Kutub al-Sittah, the six most highly regarded Sunni hadith collections. Among al-Bukhārī's other extant works are al-Tarikh al-Kabir and al-Adab al-Mufrad.

Sources of biography
Al-Bukhari's life is reconstructed primarily from contemporary accounts and biographical compendia written in the 3rd–4th centuries AH (9th–10th centuries CE).
The single most important source is Shamāʾil al-Bukhārī, a now-lost monograph by his personal scribe Abū Jaʿfar al-Warrāq, documenting al-Bukhari's life. Al-Warrāq's association with him spanned two periods: before 239 AH until al-Bukhari's second journey to Iraq (~243 AH), and from his return to Bukhara in 253 AH until shortly before his death in 256 AH. The work combined al-Warrāq's eyewitness accounts with external reports of events from other people, and circulated in two successive recensions, the second containing substantial additions.
Other early contemporary notices include Aḥmad ibn Sayyār al-Marwazī's (d. 268 AH) lost history of Khurasan, the earliest mention of al-Bukhari, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim's Al-Jarḥ wa-al-Taʿdīl (d. 327 AH), the earliest surviving notice, covering his stay in Rayy and the theological dispute over recitation of the Quran. Specialized narrator compendia of his biography include Ibn ʿAdī's (d. 365 AH) Mashāyikh al-Bukhārī, alongside notices by al-Nasāʾī (d. 303 AH), Ibn Yūnus al-Miṣrī (d. 347 AH), Ibn Ḥibbān (d. 354 AH), Ibn al-Nadīm (d. 385 AH), and Abū Aḥmad al-Ḥākim (d. 378 AH).
Though lost today, the Shamāʾil was extensively cited in the major biographic compendia of al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī (d. 463 AH), Ibn ʿAsākir (d. 571 AH), and al-Samʿānī. Both recensions were utilized by al-Dhahabī (d. 748 AH) across his historical works, and served as Ibn Ḥajar's main source for the biographical introduction of Hady al-Sari.

grok_lead: Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari (810â870 CE) was a Persian Muslim scholar and traditionist renowned for compiling Sahih al-Bukhari, a collection of approximately 7,000 prophetic hadith s deemed authentic through rigorous scrutiny of transmission chains. Born on 13 Shawwal 194 AH (20 July 810 CE) in Bukhara, then part of the Abbasid Caliphate, al-Bukhari orphaned early but inherited scholarly inclination from his father, a hadith expert, and displayed prodigious memory by age ten, having memorized the Quran and thousands of narrations. From adolescence, he embarked on extensive travels across the Islamic worldâincluding regions of modern-day Iraq, Syria, Egypt, and Hijazâspending over two decades seeking out narrators to verify hadiths against fabricated or weak reports, reportedly examining up to 600,000 traditions before selecting those with unbroken, reliable chains of transmission. His methodology emphasized not only the integrity of narrators but also their precision and orthodoxy, resulting in a work structured thematically around Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and ethics, which Sunni scholars regard as second in authority only to the Quran. In later years, al-Bukhari faced scholarly disputes in Nishapur over interpretations of divine attributes, leading to temporary exile, before settling near Samarkand, where he died on 1 Shawwal 256 AH (1 September 870 CE) and was buried in Khartank.
